SCHTEACH.TITLE: Intro to Clinical Reasoning
SCHTEACH.TECHMAT:
Small Group Assignment Instructions
Classroom Assignment #1: “The Diagnostic Deep Dive”
Assignment Type: Group-Based Case Analysis Purpose: To apply clinical reasoning, generate and prioritize differential diagnoses, document findings, and communicate with peers—all in a low-stakes, learning-focused format.
Learning Outcomes Supported
Learning Outcome
How It’s Addressed
LO1 – Inductive vs. Deductive Reasoning
Students analyze each case using both reasoning styles and reflect on which one feels more intuitive.
LO3 – Clinical Data Collection & EHR Documentation
Each team will create a brief clinical case scenario based on real Clinical Cases from Scientific journals [make sure to cite the source following AMA citation*] (e.g., "A 52-year-old male with chest discomfort, diaphoresis, and fatigue").
LO4 – Hypothesis Generation & Evidence-Based Support
Groups produce and defend prioritized diagnostic hypotheses, backed by peer-reviewed evidence, during discussion.
LO5 – Diagnosis Prioritization Using Frameworks
Students use decision-making tools (e.g., VINDICATE, scoring systems) to justify the most likely hypothesis.

Instructions
Small group activity. Each team will create a brief clinical case scenario based on real Clinical Cases from Scientific journals [make sure to cite the source following AMA citation*] (e.g., "A 52-year-old male with chest discomfort, diaphoresis, and fatigue").Stage 1 – Data Gathering: After selecting a case divided as Chief complaint, HPI, PMH, Social history, Review of System, and Physical examination. Stage 2 – Reasoning Styles: As a group, analyze the case using both inductive and deductive methods. Write a 1-paragraph summary for each reasoning style applied.Stage 3 – Hypothesis Generation: Create a list of 3 differential diagnoses and prioritize them using a decision-making tool (e.g., VINDICATE, SNAPPS, or a basic scoring system).Stage 4 – Discussion Round: Share your team's conclusions in a structured classroom discussion. Each member must explain part of the group’s reasoning and provide evidence to support. Create 10 bullet points after the discussion. Stage 5 – Reflection: Each group will submit a brief reflection (150–200 words) answering:What reasoning method felt most intuitive and why?What part of the diagnosis process challenged you the most?Stage 6- VIDEO: Create a PPT, a script, and elaborate a Panopto video of 10 minutes long and submit it on Bright Space. Evaluation Rubric
Evaluation Area
1 = Needs Work
2 = Developing
3 = Strong Performance
Data integration
Struggles to link symptoms, history, and findings
Links key elements but misses subtleties
Connect all relevant data into a coherent picture
Reasoning style
Struggles with identifying both types of reasoning
Uses only one style but has gaps
Uses both and demonstrates it in the case
Hypothesis selection
No rational or unsupported choice
Choosing a hypothesis with basic reasoning
Uses a framework/tool to select the most likely hypothesis
Differential diagnosis list
Limited or unrelated options
Mostly relevant with logical ordering
Three well-supported, prioritized differentials
Discussion round
No structure, no systematic, no organized
Some structure, some systematic, but not well organized
Structured, organized, systematic.
Reflection
The students could not answer either of the two questions correctly.
An incomplete answer or only one question was answered correctly
Complete both questions appropriately for the case study
Reasoning clarity in the video
Communication is unclear or lacks structure
Explains reasoning with some gaps
Clearly articulates decisions and supporting logic
Script and PPT
Not well structured of the case, no citation.
Some organization on the case presentation- no citation.
Well-structured case: brief clinical case scenario based on real Clinical Cases from Scientific journals [cited the source following AMA citation*]
Total X/100
8 points = 25/100
16 points 66.66 /100
24 points = 100 /100

*AMA citation example: Smith J, Doe A. Managing Hypertension in Primary Care. J Clin Med. 2020;15(4):123-129. doi:10.1001/jclinmed.2020.12345

SCHTEACH.TITLE: Genetics and Pathophysiology
SCHTEACH.SYLLABUS: nathalie.chacon/schteach/PHAS 5200 Genetics and Physiology of Health and Disease --2.pdf
SCHTEACH.PEDINN: The use of AI in the classroom. These activities engage PA students in critical thinking and practical application and help them explore complex and open-ended questions, fostering a deeper understanding of genetics and physiology in a clinical context.
SCHTEACH.TECHMAT:
Suggested Approaches to Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technologies

We will use ChatGPT in the classroom to engage students in critical thinking activities. You will learn about how to appropriately use it for physiology, when to use it for your learning and future practice, and how to cite or reference it. These activities engage PA students in critical thinking and practical application and help them explore complex and open-ended questions, fostering a deeper understanding of genetics and physiology in a clinical context.

Activity 1: Major Question Identification and ChatGPT Response Individual Question Identification Task: Ask each student to identify a significant question or challenge about genetics or physiology that ChatGPT could write. The question should be complex and open-ended, without a clear, correct answer. Examples might include:
"What are the ethical implications of genetic editing in human embryos?" "How does chronic alcohol consumption affect genetic expression related to liver function?" ChatGPT Response Task: Have students use ChatGPT to write a response to their identified question.
Activity 2: Prompt Competition Major Question Identification Task: In small teams, have students identify a significant question or challenge in genetics or physiology for ChatGPT to address. The question should be complex and debatable. Examples might include:
"What is the role of epigenetics in the development of chronic diseases?" "How should genetic information be used in personalized medicine?" Criteria Development Task: Have students collaborate in teams to develop 5 to 10 criteria for assessing ChatGPT responses. Criteria might include:
Coverage of multiple theoretical perspectives Depth of analysis Use of current research and references Clarity and coherence of the argument Ethical considerations discussed Prompt Writing Task: Ask each student to write a prompt for ChatGPT to answer the significant question their team identified.
Peer Evaluation Task: Students use the criteria they developed to judge the responses generated by ChatGPT for the prompts created by their peers. They will rate the responses from best to worst, providing constructive feedback.
Activity 3: Debate Preparation and Execution Debate Preparation Task: Divide students into pairs or small teams and assign a significant question or challenge in genetics or physiology to debate. Topics could include:
"Should gene therapy be used to treat genetic disorders in children?" "Is genetic screening for predisposition to diseases ethical in prenatal care?" ChatGPT Use: Decide if students can use ChatGPT to help prepare their opening statements and arguments.
Debate Execution Task: Have the students engage in a structured debate, presenting their arguments and counterarguments. Ensure each side has equal time to present and rebut.
Debrief and Reflection Task: After the debate, conduct a debriefing session where students reflect on the arguments presented, the effectiveness of their preparation, and the insights gained from considering multiple perspectives.
Integration of Bloom's Taxonomy Knowledge: Identify critical terms and concepts in genetics and physiology relevant to the activities. Comprehension: Explain underlying principles and mechanisms, such as genetic inheritance patterns or physiological responses to deficiencies. Application: Apply theoretical knowledge to practical scenarios like case studies or genetic counseling simulations. Analysis: Analyze complex scenarios, such as ethical implications or the interplay between genetic factors and environmental influences. Synthesis: Formulate comprehensive treatment plans or genetic counseling strategies that integrate various aspects of patient care. Evaluation: Critically evaluate treatment strategies, ethical dilemmas, and ChatGPT-generated responses based on predefined criteria.
SCHTEACH.ENHSTUD: Use of AI in the classroom. These activities engage PA students in critical thinking and practical application and help them explore complex and open-ended questions, fostering a deeper understanding of genetics and physiology in a clinical context.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Curricular Innovations through OER Grant Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
LEVEL-UP: Evaluation Tool for Gamification in Health Professions Education
Nahtalie Chacon, Christina Gonzales Julian Garza and Angelica Urbina
Gamified learning strategies are increasingly used in health professions didactic education to promote engagement and application of knowledge; however, there is no standardized, openly available method for students to consistently evaluate the quality and educational impact of these activities. Faculty often rely on informal feedback, limiting the ability to compare activities, refine instructional design, or scale effective practices. This project will develop an Open Educational Resource (OER): a standardized, student-reported evaluation tool for gamified learning activities in health professions didactic education. The tool will assess key domains of high-quality experiential learning, including engagement, instructional design, cognitive challenge, teamwork, accessibility, and perceived learning outcomes, with design and implementation guided by ADA accessibility standards, supporting evidence-informed curricular improvement. This work is timely as health professions programs continue to redesign didactic curricula to emphasize integration, active learning, and student success. By openly licensing this evaluation tool, the project aligns with UT System priorities to advance curricular innovation, reduce barrier

CONGRANT.TITLE: UT System Curricular Innovation through Open Educational Resources (OER) Grant Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
UnlockED: An Escape Room Learning Toolkit for Higher Education
Angelica Urbina, Christina Gonzles and Nathalie Chacon
Gamified learning strategies are increasingly used in higher education to promote student engagement and application of knowledge. This proposal seeks to develop UnlockED, an openly licensed Escape Room Learning Toolkit designed as a PDF reference manual with visuals and step-by-step instructions to guide faculty and educators in creating and implementing effective educational escape rooms as an active-learning strategy. The project builds on the authors' extensive experience designing and implementing both classroom-based and digital escape rooms across multiple courses to support collaboration, problem-solving, and application-based learning. Currently, these escape room activities exist as instructor-specific implementations; this project addresses the need for a structured, step-by-step Open Educational Resource (OER) that guides others through the design, facilitation, and curricular integration of escape rooms.
The proposed toolkit aligns with the UT System's Curricular Innovation through OER Grant Program by advancing open pedagogy, reducing barriers to adoption of active-learning practices, and supporting scalable curricular innovation. The applicant team brings demonstrated expertise in curriculum design, gamified instruction, and digital resource development, positioning them with the capacity to successfully develop, implement, and disseminate a sustainable toolkit.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Long COVID as a Chronic Multisystem Disorder: Pathogenesis, Persistence, and Therapeutic Perspectives
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In October 2021, the WHO defined Long COVID, or post‑acute sequelae of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection (PASC), as a condition characterized by symptoms that persist for at least two months, typically beginning three months after the acute infection and not attributable to alternative diagnoses. Long COVID is now recognized as a chronic, multisystem disorder encompassing more than 200 reported symptoms across respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurological, and systemic domains. Increasing evidence indicates that persistent SARS‑CoV‑2 activity within sanctuary tissues—including lymphoid organs, the gastrointestinal tract, and the olfactory neuroepithelium—may sustain chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation long after viral clearance from the upper airways. Persistent viral proteins can disrupt cellular homeostasis, impair organelle function, and trigger apoptosis, while endothelial dysfunction has emerged as a central driver of systemic manifestations. Detection of sub genomic viral RNA, residual viral proteins, and sustained antigenemia supports the hypothesis of ongoing low‑level replication or delayed clearance in a subset of patients. Such persistence may also facilitate reactivation of latent herpesviruses, particularly Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), which establishes lifelong latency in B lymphocytes. EBV reactivation has been increasingly documented during acute COVID‑19 and may contribute both to severe disease endotypes and to post‑acute symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive impairment, and neuropsychiatric disturbances. This review synthesizes current evidence linking viral persistence, immune dysregulation, endothelial injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and herpesvirus reactivation as interconnected mechanisms driving Long COVID pathogenesis, highlighting the need for targeted diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

SARS-CoV-2: Potential feco-oral transmission and implications on the spread and severity of COVID-19 in Venezuela. Mini-review
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The recognized human-to-human transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is through respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces. However, the high transmissibility of the virus and the pattern of symptoms of COVID-19 suggest the likelihood of other forms of spread. Increasing evidence suggests that SARS‐CoV‐2 could be transmitted by the feco‐oral route. SARS-CoV-2 is known to infect gastrointestinal epithelial cells and a significant number of infected people have gastrointestinal symptoms. Viable viruses, viral RNA, and prolonged shedding of viral RNA have been detected in the feces of COVID-19 patients. The virus has been found in sewage and surface waters of several countries. The possible feco-oral transmission of SARS-CoV-2 could be significant in low-income countries. High poverty levels and the collapse of health and other public services might increase the risk of Venezuelans to suffer a more devastating impact from COVID-19 than other populations. In conclusion, the feco-oral transmission of SARS-CoV-2 has not been demonstrated. However, it is conceivable and the impact of COVID-19 could be high in low-income countries, especially in Venezuela due to its humanitarian crisis. The lack of information on the viability and infectivity of the virus in wastewaters and surface waters and the risk of transmission of the infection are important gaps in knowledge that deserve further investigation.

PRESENT.TITLE: Epstein-Barr virus reactivation as a driver of Long COVID Mechanism, biomarkers and trial-ready interventions
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Evidence suggests a potential EBV-associated severity endotype in COVID‑19, with PCR-defined EBV reactivation commonly reported in severe/ICU populations, but with substantial heterogeneity across studies and specimen types. [Su Y, 2022], [Talukder, 2024]. Across included reviews/meta-analyses, there was no pooled OR/RR/HR specifically linking PCR EBV DNAemia to subsequent development of PASC/Long COVID, indicating an important evidence gap at the umbrella-review level [bmj, 2017], [Su Y, 2022], [Talukder, 2024]. Longitudinal cohort evidence referenced within the included reviews indicates that EBV viremia at diagnosis may anticipate post‑acute symptom outcomes (including fatigue and cognitive/memory symptoms), supporting biological plausibility but requiring replication with standardized PCR protocols. [Su Y, 2022], [bmj.com, 2017], [Su Y, 2022]. Supportive acute-outcome evidence shows higher mortality risk in EBV+/COVID+ versus EBV−/COVID+ hospitalized cohorts, consistent with EBV reactivation as a severity marker/endotype rather than direct proof of Long COVID causation [Talukder, 2024]. Future studies should use prospective longitudinal designs with standardized EBV DNAemia measurements and consistent Long COVID definitions to determine EBV’s clinical and therapeutic relevance.

PRESENT.NAME: RGV Society Annual Conference
PRESENT.TITLE: Decoding Long COVID: Risk Factors, Proteomics, and Treatment
PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
Abstract: Long COVID or Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), is a chronic disorder characterized by persistent symptoms and health issues following SARS-CoV2 infection. This conference aims to provide a comprehensive overview and new theories of Long COVID, focusing on its definition, diagnosis criteria, symptoms, risk factors, and pathophysiology. We consider that Long COVID is a systemic disorder that includes the endothelial tissue as its modulator of the disease expression, viral persistence in patients with prior conditions, autoimmunity, and coagulopathies are part of the underlying pathology. We will explore the natural history of the disease, proteomic insights, and both conventional and non-conventional treatment approaches. Long COVID requires a full study to understand the best treatment option based on the infection timeline, which risk factor defines progression to Long COVID and prognosis biomarkers. Finally, we will discuss future steps in research and clinical practice to manage better and understand this condition.

Purpose of Presentation
This interdisciplinary presentation aimed to advance understanding of Long COVID by integrating virology, immunology, proteomics, and clinical treatment strategies. It emphasized the importance of early diagnosis, biomarker identification, and personalized care approaches.

Key Scientific Contributions
Pathogenesis & Immunopathophysiology:
Long COVID is characterized by persistent viral presence, immune dysregulation, oxidative stress, endothelial damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
The disease affects multiple organ systems and is driven by cycles of inflammation, thrombosis, and autoimmunity.Risk Factors Identified: Female sex, middle age Severe acute infection Low vitamin D levels EBV reactivation Comorbidities Protective Factors: Vaccination Early antiviral therapy Physical activity Vitamin D sufficiency Proteomics & Biomarker Discovery
Proteomic analysis revealed host-virus protein interactions and novel therapeutic targets. Key biomarkers include IL-6, TNF-α, CRP, HMGB1, low taurine, and mitochondrial damage indicators. The interactome of SARS-CoV-2 proteins with host pathways (e.g., ACE2, TMPRSS2, NRP1) was mapped to guide future drug development.
This presentation is part of a broader research initiative and will contribute to the future peer-reviewed publications.

PRESENT.NAME: 2023 UTRGV COHP Inter professional Education Symposium
PRESENT.TITLE: PILOT RESULTS FROM STUDYING INTERPROFESSIONAL COLLABORATION PERCEPTIONS AMONG HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Traditional healthcare has been characterized as a field where professionals work independently, creating an environment with multiple providers in multiple locations duplicating services, adding to the ineffectiveness and waste of resources. The fragmentation of healthcare provision promotes isolation, competition, and attempts to preserve power among professions. Accordingly, patient care is less than optimum. To begin to ameliorate this situation Interprofessional Education has been developed. However, a significant part of this education is effective interprofessional collaboration (IPC) which creates higher patient satisfaction, better coordination of patient care, efficient use of healthcare services, and higher professional job satisfaction. Furthermore, the World Health Organization has made collaboration a priority based on Health Ethics. The purpose of this research is to determine the differences in healthcare professionals’ perceptions of IPC, demographic factors related to IPC, and what dimensions and aspects of IPC healthcare rate the highest. The significance of this survey research is the provision of information and a starting point for the groundwork for the interprofessional education of pre-health care professionals. The participant sample consists of physician assistants, nursing, occupational therapists, communication sciences and disorders, health, and biomedical sciences, health, and human performance, social work, cooperative pharmacy, and rehabilitation counseling. The Perception of Interprofessional Collaboration Model-Questionnaire (PINCOM- Q) is the survey instrument used in this study. Keywords: Interprofessional collaboration, interprofessional education, global, healthcare, fragmentation, healthcare ethics
